01.event: Rabbi Elazar missed the study hall one day and asked Rabbi Asi what had been said there.
01.turn: Rabbi Asi reported Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
01.outcome: Rabbi Elazar learned the ruling and drew an inference from it.
01.summary: Rabbi Elazar did not attend the study hall one day. Meeting Rabbi Asi, he asked what the Sages had said, and Rabbi Asi told him Rabbi Yochanan ruled like Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Elazar inferred from this that some individual must disagree, and Rabbi Asi confirmed it.
01.missing: The exchange is mostly a vehicle for transmitting a ruling; little happens beyond the question and answer.

02.actor: Rabbi Zeira's neighbors and a gentile superintendent
02.event: A gentile superintendent refused to rent his domain to his Jewish neighbors for an eiruv, so they asked Rabbi Zeira whether they could rent it from his wife.
02.turn: Rabbi Zeira cited Rabbi Hanina's ruling that a man's wife may make an eiruv without his knowledge.
02.outcome: The neighbors were permitted to rent the domain from the wife.
02.summary: A gentile official living near Rabbi Zeira refused to rent his property to the neighbors so they could carry on Shabbat. They asked Rabbi Zeira whether they could rent it from his wife instead. He answered, citing Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Hanina, that a wife may establish an eiruv without her husband's knowledge, so they could.

03.actor: A man whose betrothed died; Rav Nahman's circle; Rav Hiyya bar Ami
03.event: A man whose betrothed had died came before the sages, who told him to bury her or pay her marriage contract.
03.turn: Rav Hiyya bar Ami objected, citing a teaching that a man has no mourning or inheritance obligations for a betrothed wife.
03.summary: Several sages were sitting together when a man came whose betrothed wife had died. They told him to bury her or pay her marriage contract. Rav Hiyya bar Ami challenged them with a mishna stating that a betrothed husband neither mourns nor inherits from her. The text does not say what the man finally did.
03.missing: How the case was resolved for the man; the passage turns into legal analysis.

04.actor: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok and his family, descendants of Sena'av ben Binyamin
04.event: When the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat, the family postponed the fast to Sunday.
04.turn: Sunday was their family festival day.
04.outcome: They fasted but did not complete the fast because of their festival.
04.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recalled that his family, descendants of Sena'av ben Binyamin, kept a family festival. Once the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat and the fast was pushed to Sunday, which was their festival. They fasted that day but broke off before evening because it was their holiday.

05.event: Rav came to Damharya and issued a practical ruling about a breach in an alleyway.
05.turn: Rav Hanan bar Rava argued the ruling was a special stringency because Rav found an unguarded valley.
05.summary: Rav Huna claimed that Rav, visiting Damharya, had ruled according to Rav Huna's view. Rav Hanan bar Rava replied that Rav had found the place lax and added a safeguard there. The incident is only cited as evidence in a legal dispute.
05.missing: The details of the Damharya incident itself; it is only alluded to.

06.actor: A man who fell into the Great Cistern
06.event: A man fell into the Great Cistern and emerged after three days.
06.outcome: He survived, which the Sages called a miracle not to be used for halakha.
06.summary: Rabbi Meir cited the case of a man who fell into a great cistern and came out alive three days later. The Sages replied that one does not cite miracles as legal precedent. The incident itself is only referenced, not told.
06.missing: The narrative of the fall and rescue is only mentioned by reference to the mishna.

07.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch
07.event: A man betrothed a woman in the marketplace with a myrtle branch, and Rav Aha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef.
07.turn: Rav Yosef ruled the man should be flogged and the woman should need a divorce.
07.outcome: The man was to be flogged per Rav, and a bill of divorce required per Shmuel.
07.summary: A man betrothed a woman in the marketplace using a myrtle branch. Rav Aha bar Huna sent the question to Rav Yosef. Rav Yosef replied that the man should be flogged for his crude conduct, and that the woman needed a bill of divorce in case the branch had some value.

08.event: People came before Rabbi Ami with a bill of divorce lacking witnesses.
08.outcome: He told them to complete it even with a slave from the market.
08.summary: People brought Rabbi Ami a case of a bill of divorce that needed more witnesses. He told them to go and complete it even with a slave from the public. It is a bare report of a ruling.
08.missing: Who came and what the case was is only implied.

09.event: The Rabbis urged Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons.
09.turn: He replied that his daughter's sons were his sons, but in truth he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long discourses.
09.outcome: He put them off and did not remarry.
09.summary: The Rabbis told Rav Sheshet he should marry and father sons. He answered that his grandsons through his daughter counted as his sons. The Gemara explains he was only deflecting them: he had become impotent from waiting through Rav Huna's very long lectures.

10.actor: A depositor and the family of Rabbi Meyasha
10.event: A man deposited seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without telling his household whose they were.
10.turn: Rabbi Ami knew Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy, and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
10.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the claimant.
10.summary: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet at the home of Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rabbi Meyasha died without saying whose they were, and the dispute came to Rabbi Ami. He ruled for the claimant, since he knew Rabbi Meyasha could not have afforded such gems and the claimant could describe them.

11.event: Shimon ben Azzai found a genealogy scroll in Jerusalem.
11.turn: It recorded a mamzer, praise of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings, and that Manasseh killed Isaiah.
11.summary: Shimon ben Azzai reported finding a scroll of lineages in Jerusalem. Among its entries were that a certain man was a mamzer, that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings were few but reliable, and that King Manasseh killed the prophet Isaiah. Beyond the finding, the passage is a list of contents.
11.missing: The Manasseh-Isaiah story is only stated as a fact here; its telling begins in the following segment.

12.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
12.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land, and Rav bought it for himself.
12.turn: The land lay among violent people who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rav feared someone else would buy it meanwhile.
12.outcome: Rav kept the land without first informing Rabba bar bar Hana.
12.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a field for him, but Rav bought it for himself. The Gemara explains that the field was in a valley of violent men who would sell to Rav but not to Rabba bar bar Hana. Rav did not stop to tell him first, fearing that another buyer would get it in the meantime.

13.event: In a good mood, Abaye boasted that he was like ben Azzai, ready for any question.
13.turn: A Sage challenged him on why the redemption verses are read leniently.
13.outcome: Abaye answered from the Torah's leniency toward a Hebrew slave; the debate continues.
13.summary: Abaye once declared himself as sharp as ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias. A scholar immediately tested him: why read the verses about redeeming a Hebrew slave leniently rather than stringently? Abaye answered that the Torah is consistently lenient toward such a slave. The rest is legal argument.
13.missing: The exchange has no narrative ending; it continues as legal debate.

14.event: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer and then Rabbi Yehoshua whom to serve first if both parents ask for water.
14.turn: When he asked about a divorced mother, Rabbi Yehoshua saw from his tearful eyes that he was a widow's son.
14.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua answered him sarcastically to pour water in a basin and call them like chickens.
14.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer whether father or mother comes first if both ask for water, and was told the father. He asked Rabbi Yehoshua and got the same answer, then asked what if the mother were divorced. Rabbi Yehoshua noticed his tear-filled eyes, realized he had no living father, and mocked the pointless question: pour water in a bowl and cluck for them like chickens.

15.event: Rabbi Shabbtai's widowed daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag full of coins for her sustenance.
15.outcome: The Sages had no power to take it from her.
15.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law grabbed a saddlebag full of coins to support herself. The Sages found they had no legal authority to take it back from her.

16.actor: Two claimants to a field and Rav Yosef
16.event: Two deeds of sale for the same property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan'.
16.turn: Rav Yosef awarded the field to the dated deed, and the loser asked for an authorization to repossess from Iyyar on.
16.outcome: Rav Yosef refused, since buyers could claim his deed was from the first of Nisan.
16.summary: Two men brought Rav Yosef deeds to the same field, one dated the fifth of Nisan, the other only 'Nisan'. Rav Yosef gave it to the man with the exact date. The loser protested and asked for a writ letting him seize property sold from Iyyar on, but Rav Yosef answered that buyers could say his deed was from the first of Nisan and so the field was his to chase.

17.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
17.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to test whether he would become angry.
17.summary: Rav Huna deliberately tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether the son would lose his temper. The Gemara discusses whether this was permitted, noting he had waived his honor. The text does not say how the son reacted.
17.missing: The son's reaction and how the test ended.

18.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
18.event: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua conducted a halitza before five judges.
18.outcome: They did so to publicize the matter.
18.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua performed a halitza ceremony with five judges rather than three. The Gemara explains they did this only to make the event publicly known. It is a bare report of a practice.

19.event: Rav Yehuda ruled in a case about a bundle of branches.
19.outcome: He treated it as consumption of the wife's property.
19.summary: The judges of Pumbedita reported that Rav Yehuda once decided a case involving bundles of vine branches. The ruling is cited only to show his consistent legal view.
19.missing: The facts of the case are supplied by the translation, not the text.

20.actor: A man who sold land to Rav Pappa
20.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money to buy oxen.
20.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
20.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land to him, beyond the letter of the law.
20.summary: A man sold a field to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen. In the end he did not need the money, and Rav Pappa gave him back his land. The Gemara notes Rav Pappa did this beyond what the law required.
